label: Linear Inequalities in One Variable
overview: Solving a linear inequality follows the same steps as solving an equation, with one critical rule: multiplying or dividing by a negative number flips the inequality sign. SAT questions ask you to solve, graph on a number line, or interpret the solution in context (e.g., 'what is the minimum number of items...').

keyFormulas.name: Solving inequality
keyFormulas.latex: ax + b > c \implies x > \dfrac{c-b}{a} \quad (\text{flip if } a < 0)

keyFormulas.name: Flip rule
keyFormulas.latex: \text{If you multiply/divide by a negative, flip } > \text{ to } <

steps.title: Divide by −2 and flip the inequality
steps.content: Dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality direction.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when dividing by a negative
commonMistakes.fix: Any time you divide (or multiply) both sides by a negative number, the inequality reverses: < becomes >, ≤ becomes ≥.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a closed circle for a strict inequality (< or >)
commonMistakes.fix: Strict inequalities (< or >) use an open circle. Non-strict (≤ or ≥) use a closed (filled) circle.

quickTip: After solving, test a value in the solution set back in the original inequality to confirm your answer is correct.
